title: SiGeo: Sub-One-Shot NAS via Geometry of Loss Landscape

problem.claim: NAS aims to automate neural network design, but existing one-shot methods often require extensive training and zero-shot methods cannot use training-improvement information and may perform unreliably on complex domains.

gap.claim: A NAS approach is needed that combines the lower computational requirements of zero-shot methods with information from limited training, while improving reliability in complex settings.

contributions.claim: Introduces a sub-one-shot NAS paradigm that bridges zero-shot and one-shot NAS by warming up a supernet on only a small subset of training data.
Presents SiGeo, a proxy for sub-one-shot NAS founded on a theoretical framework connecting supernet warm-up with proxy efficacy.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe the theoretical framework connecting supernet warm-up with proxy efficacy as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that, when properly warmed up, SiGeo surpasses state-of-the-art NAS proxies across many established computer-vision NAS benchmarks.
The authors report that SiGeo matches state-of-the-art weight-sharing one-shot NAS methods on recommendation-system benchmarks while reducing computational costs by approximately 60%.

narrative_sequence.summary: NAS is widely used to automate neural network design.
One-shot NAS requires extensive training, while zero-shot NAS lacks training-improvement information and can be unreliable in complex domains.
The authors introduce sub-one-shot NAS, using limited supernet warm-up, and propose the SiGeo proxy with a theoretical warm-up framework.
The authors report strong benchmark results in computer vision and recommendation systems, including approximately 60% lower computational cost in the latter.

source_observation.claim: Limited supernet warm-up is presented as a way to retain training-derived information while using less computation than extensive one-shot training.

interpretation.claim: A small amount of targeted training may provide a useful middle ground between training-free proxies and fully trained weight-sharing methods.

application.claim: For architecture-search settings where full training is expensive but zero-shot proxies are unreliable, evaluate proxies after a controlled warm-up phase.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish how much warm-up is required or whether the approach generalizes beyond the reported benchmarks and domains.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the theoretical framework, proxy formulation, or warm-up schedule.
The abstract does not provide benchmark names, quantitative accuracy results, or experimental baselines beyond broad method categories.
The abstract does not detail the conditions under which the approximately 60% computational-cost reduction was measured.
